text: Pillar three is a Python script, and it has to check access two different ways on each cloud, not one. Hartwell's break-glass procedure has, in the past, granted a handful of accounts direct, individually-assigned admin access to the OT SCADA boundary, bypassing the groups entirely. A script that only checks group membership would never see those accounts at all.

On the Entra ID side, one call pages through the SCADA-OT-Admins group's members using the Graph API. A separate call checks Azure Resource Manager role assignments scoped directly to the SCADA resource group, filtered down to direct user assignments of the SCADA Operator role -- the exact gap group membership alone would miss.

On the AWS side, the same split applies. get_group returns who's in the scada-ot-admins group. A completely separate call, list_entities_for_policy with EntityFilter set to User, returns exactly which users have the SCADA Emergency Access policy attached directly -- it does not include anyone who only has that access through the group.

Every account from all four queries gets normalized into one record with an access_path field: group_membership or direct_assignment. The union of all of them becomes the total count of accounts with standing SCADA access, and the direct-assignment-only count is exactly the population a group-only review will never catch. The normalized records get written into a Sentinel custom log table, ScadaAccessInventory_CL, so the inventory is queryable, not a one-off script run. Next lesson gets this running on a schedule, in production.
